# Was this video most likely shot handheld?

**Yes. This was almost certainly shot handheld.** I measured the camera's motion
frame by frame rather than judging it by eye, and the numbers are decisive: the
camera rolls, sways and drifts in ways that a tripod, slider or gimbal physically
cannot reproduce.

## The clip and the method

The file is 6.67 s, 640×360, 59.94 fps, H.264. I first confirmed that no frames
are duplicated (every consecutive pair differs; the minimum inter-frame
difference is well above zero), so this is genuine 59.94p and the per-frame
motion figures below are real camera movement rather than frame-rate padding.

I then estimated global camera motion between every pair of frames by
phase-correlating a grid of image tiles and fitting a robust affine model
(translation, rotation and scale) to the tile displacements. A closure test —
comparing the direct frame k→k+2 estimate against the sum of the two single-frame
steps — puts the precision of this estimator at about 0.06–0.08 px. That number
matters, because the effects described below are ten to a hundred times larger
than it.

The shot itself: a slow move to the right across a queue of life-size sculpted
figures in a dim gallery (mean luminance 42/255), with a very near figure filling
the left of the frame and the queue receding to small, distant figures and a far
wall at the right. The camera moves rightward from roughly t=0.8 s to t=3.9 s,
covering about 140 px, and then appears to settle and hold for the final 2.7
seconds.

## The decisive evidence: the camera rolls while it is supposedly locked off

The last 2.7 seconds, when the operator has stopped moving and is holding a
framing, is exactly where a tripod would give itself away. It does the opposite.

I measured roll by phase-correlating the left third and the right third of the
frame separately against their own position at t=4.0 s and taking the difference
in their vertical displacement over the 384 px that separates them. Over the
"static" hold the image rotates smoothly from +0.25° through zero to −0.23°: a
total roll excursion of **0.48°**, with a standard deviation of 0.12°. It is a
slow, continuous rocking, not noise.

**A tripod pan/tilt head has no roll axis at all.** The camera is bolted to a
plate; there is no mechanism by which it can rock half a degree back and forth
while sitting on sticks. Nor can a slider, dolly or jib roll the camera. Only a
hand, wrist or shoulder can.

I checked that this roll is not an artifact of the scene's depth: a vertical
camera sway would, through parallax, make near content shift slightly more than
far content and could masquerade as roll. Given the measured parallax strength
and the size of the vertical sway, that mechanism could fake at most 0.025° —
nineteen times smaller than what I measured. The roll also correlates only weakly
(r = +0.43) with the vertical sway, which it would have to track almost perfectly
if it were a depth artifact. The roll is real.

## The "hold" at the end never actually holds still

Over those same final 2.7 seconds, the framing wanders continuously. Measured
against the frame at t=4.0 s, it creeps right to about +3.8 px, drifts back
through zero and carries on to −2.5 px, while sliding about 4.5 px vertically —
a total excursion of roughly **7 px horizontally and 4.6 px vertically**, with
standard deviations of 1.7 px and 1.2 px. The mean speed of this drift is
0.14 px/frame, about 8 px/s, or 1.3% of the frame width every second.

Three things confirm this is genuine camera motion and not measurement error.
First, it is 20 to 100 times the estimator's 0.08 px noise floor. Second, the
trajectory is smooth and reverses direction several times, which noise does not
do. Third, and most convincingly, I repeated the measurement with three
non-overlapping windows — the left, centre and right thirds of the frame, sharing
no pixels — and they produced essentially the same trajectory: the horizontal
paths correlate at r = 0.998 and the vertical paths at r = 0.94–0.97.

A camera locked to a tripod would sit within a fraction of a pixel for 2.7
seconds. What this clip does instead is the unmistakable slow float of a person
trying, and not quite managing, to hold a frame still.

## The move itself behaves like an unconstrained mount

**Pitch, yaw and roll all wander independently.** During the rightward move the
frame also rises about 36 px and accumulates about 1.4° of roll, and then keeps
that roll rather than correcting it. Crucially, none of these track each other.
The roll sits near −0.3° through the first half of the horizontal move and only
then dives to −1.4°; most of the vertical rise is crammed into one short stretch
while the horizontal speed is unchanged. This rules out the one way a tripod can
appear to roll — an unlevelled tripod, which produces roll in strict proportion
to the pan angle. Here roll is plainly not proportional to yaw. Three axes moving
independently means nothing was constraining them.

**The velocity is irregular.** Horizontal speed hovers around 1.0 px/frame but

acceleration or deceleration envelope, and the vertical speed fluctuates on its
own schedule. A fluid head, even an inexpensive one, damps exactly this kind of
variation and delivers a far more uniform sweep.

is dominated by low frequencies (70% of its energy below 3 Hz — body and postural
sway), while horizontal jitter and roll each carry roughly a quarter of their
energy up in the 8–15 Hz band. That high band is the classic signature of human
physiological tremor transmitted through a camera body, and a tripod has no
mechanism that could generate a persistent broadband wobble like it, least of all

artifact of the tiles losing their content as the frame moved, and the 6% above

The embedded title tag identifies it as B-roll footage ("Victory for the Net"). Nothing in the scene moves, so every change in framing is camera motion. I also cross-checked the totals with direct comparisons between distant frames (e.g. first vs last frame), which match the accumulated trajectory.

## Why it is handheld

1. **The camera moves in a way that is deliberate but irregular.** The shot is a slow pan: the image content slides about 140 px to the left (the camera turns right) and about 30 px up (the camera tilts down slightly) between roughly 0.6 s and 3.9 s, then the camera holds on the new framing for the remaining 2.7 s. That is an operator following a row of figures and settling, not a locked-off camera (which would show zero motion) and not a still photograph-style shot.

2. **The pan velocity is not constant or smoothly ramped.** A motorized pan head or slider produces a clean trapezoidal velocity profile. Here the horizontal velocity oscillates between about 22 and 66 px/s during the move (standard deviation 23% of the mean), with visible undulations of roughly 0.7 to 1 s period. Before the pan even starts, the camera drifts a few pixels the opposite way (right and down) in the first 0.4 s and then reverses into the pan. That small counter-drift and "wind-up" is typical of a human hand starting a move.

3. **There is a sudden vertical lurch during the pan.** Around 2.9 to 3.2 s the frame drops about 20 px in a third of a second (vertical velocity briefly reaches about -45 px/s) while the horizontal pan is still running. This is the kind of jolt produced by a body adjustment, step, or regrip, not by mechanical support.

4. **The camera rolls, and the roll is not tied to the pan angle.** The horizon rotates by roughly one degree (0.6 to 1.2 degrees depending on the estimator), almost all of it between 2.5 and 3.5 s, and then wanders by a few tenths of a degree during the hold (a direct comparison of the frame at 4.2 s with the last frame gives about 0.35 degrees of roll change). A tripod head, slider, or dolly cannot roll like this; even an unlevelled tripod would produce a roll that changes smoothly and monotonically with pan angle, whereas here roll stays flat for the first two-thirds of the pan and then jumps. A 3-axis gimbal would hold roll fixed. Only a camera supported by hands and arms drifts in roll this way.

5. **The camera never sits perfectly still.** During the "hold" at the end (4.2 to 6.7 s), the framing still wanders about 6.5 px horizontally and 4.5 px vertically (confirmed by direct, non-cumulative comparisons between frames in this segment: e.g. the frame at 5.0 s and the last frame differ by about 6.5 px horizontally) with a dominant slow component near 0.4 Hz (body sway / breathing range) plus smaller 1 to 3 Hz components (arm tremor range). A tripod-mounted camera would show essentially zero motion here (well under a pixel), and any tremor would be absent rather than merely small.

6. **There is a slight zoom-in / forward drift** (scale grows about 2.5% during the move) and slightly larger displacement of the near figure at the left than of the distant background at the right. Part of this is ordinary perspective stretching during a pan, so I treat it as weak supporting evidence only. But it is consistent with the operator's body leaning or shifting forward while panning, and inconsistent with a pure nodal pan on a tripod.

## What it is not

- **Not a tripod / locked-off shot:** the frame moves continuously and the roll changes.
- **Not a slider or dolly:** the near figure (about 1 m away) and the far wall move by nearly the same amount, so the move is a rotation (pan), not a lateral translation; a slider would produce strong near/far parallax.
- **Not a motorized pan or gimbal:** the velocity is wavy, there is a lurch, and the roll drifts.

The high-frequency jitter is small (about 0.17 px frame-to-frame in the hold), which suggests either a relatively heavy camera or rig, a careful operator, or optical/electronic image stabilization taking out the fastest tremor. Stabilization would remove fine shake but leaves exactly the low-frequency drift, roll wander and lurch seen here, so it does not change the conclusion: the camera was hand-supported.

# Was this video most likely shot handheld? Why?

## Answer: No. The video was most likely not shot handheld. It looks like a stabilized / locked-off shot — a camera on a tripod, slider, or solid support — with one smooth initial reframing move, then an essentially static hold.

The clip is 6.7 s, 640x360, 400 frames at about 59.94 fps. It shows a line of statue-like figures seen from the side in a warm interior. Nothing in the scene moves; all image motion is camera motion. I extracted the full frame sequence, compared frames seconds apart and frame-to-frame at full rate, built horizontal and vertical slit-scans through the whole clip, and made amplified difference images.

What those show is the opposite of handheld character:

1. There is no continuous high-frequency jitter. Consecutive frames at 1/60 s late in the clip are visually identical. Their amplified difference is only random speckle from sensor and compression noise, with no coherent double-edges around the figures. That means inter-frame motion is a fraction of a pixel. A hand-held camera shows constant small random translation plus pitch, yaw, and roll from hands, breathing, and body sway, normally several pixels of wander with reversals and corrections, even in a careful hold.

2. The only substantial motion is a single smooth drift in one direction early in the clip. Frame 0 versus frame 60 versus frame 200 shows every figure contour displaced the same way, as bright rims on one side of edges in the difference image. A side-by-side with a fixed vertical reference shows the picture content sliding to the left by roughly 30-40 pixels over about three seconds, revealing more on the right. The slit-scan with time on the vertical axis shows lines that slant at the top and then become straight and vertical. In other words, the camera moves monotonically one way and eases to a stop; it does not wander back and forth.

3. That move has no handheld-like vertical or rotational component. The vertical slit-scan, where camera up-down or roll would tilt or wave the bands, stays flat. The horizontal wall trim stays at the same image height from first to last frame. Handheld repositioning almost always couples horizontal with vertical bobble and a little roll. Here vertical is stable to about a pixel while horizontal moves tens of pixels.

4. After the move ends, the camera stays put except for a very slow creep in the same direction. A difference between frames 200 and 400, 3.3 s apart, shows thin coherent edge ghosts, much thinner than the early one-second difference, not a random walk. The late-only slit-scan is straight-sided apart from sub-pixel serration. A handheld operator cannot hold a 60 fps image that repeatable for seconds and then creep only one way at about a pixel per second.

5. The character of the early move itself is deliberate, not shake. Its rate is on the order of 10 pixels per second and it decelerates smoothly to a hold. The foreground head appears to shift somewhat more than the distant figures, suggesting a small lateral translation component such as a short slider move, or a pan with some parallax, rather than rotational tremor. Either way it is a smooth single-axis reframing, the kind made on a fluid tripod head or slider, not a hand tremor at 8-12 Hz or body sway at fractions of a hertz.

For all these reasons — absence of persistent two-axis random jitter and roll, one smooth monotonic nearly horizontal move that decelerates to a stop, vertical stability throughout, and a multi-second near-locked hold with only slow same-direction creep — the most defensible reading is a supported, locked-off camera that is reframed once at the start, not a camera held in the hands.
